<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line" lang="en">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">MiMo-V2-Flash Technical Report</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">LLM-Core Xiaomi
</span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">We present MiMo-V2-Flash, a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model with 309B total parameters and 15B active parameters, designed for fast, strong reasoning and agentic capabilities. MiMo-V2-Flash adopts a hybrid attention architecture that interleaves <span id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Sliding Window Attention (SWA)</span> with global attention, with a 128-token sliding window under a 5:1 hybrid ratio. The model is pre-trained on 27 trillion tokens with <span id="abstract1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Multi-Token Prediction (MTP)</span>, employing a native 32k context length and subsequently extended to 256k.
To efficiently scale post-training compute, MiMo-V2-Flash introduces a novel <span id="abstract1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD)</span> paradigm.
In this framework, domain-specialized teachers (e.g., trained via large-scale reinforcement learning) provide dense and token-level reward, enabling the student model to perfectly master teacher expertise.
MiMo-V2-Flash rivals top-tier open-weight models such as DeepSeek-V3.2 and Kimi-K2, despite using only <math id="abstract1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1/2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1/2</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="abstract1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1/3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1/3</annotation></semantics></math> of their total parameters, respectively.
During inference, by repurposing MTP as a draft model for speculative decoding, MiMo-V2-Flash achieves up to 3.6 acceptance length and 2.6<math id="abstract1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> decoding speedup with three MTP layers.
We open-source both the model weights and the three-layer MTP weights to foster open research and community collaboration.</p>
  
</div>
<figure id="S0.F1" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2601.02780v2/teaser.svg" id="S0.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/232;" width="476" height="232"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S0.F1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>: </span><span id="S0.F1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Benchmark performance of MiMo-V2-Flash.</span></figcaption>
</figure>

<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Recent progress towards Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) is increasingly propelled by two frontiers: advanced reasoning chains and autonomous agentic workflows <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Google DeepMind, 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kimi Team, 2025a</a>)</cite>, grounded in large-scale Reinforcement Learning (RL).
Yet building scalable reasoners and agents hits a common critical bottleneck, where long-context modeling must be simultaneously fast and strong.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In this work, we introduce MiMo-V2-Flash, an efficient and cost-effective Large Language Model (LLM) that delivers strong reasoning and agentic performance.
MiMo-V2-Flash is a 309B-parameter MoE with 15B activated per token.
To alleviate the quadratic complexity of full attention, MiMo-V2-Flash adopts a hybrid attention mechanism that interleaves local sliding window and global attention. The sliding window size is 128-token and the hybrid local:global ratio is 5:1, yielding nearly a 6× reduction in KV-cache storage and attention computation for long contexts.
With the help of learnable attention sink bias <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Agarwal et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, the hybrid architecture maintains strong modeling capability even in long-context scenarios, despite the aggressive sliding window size and hybrid ratio.
MiMo-V2-Flash also incorporates Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) to enhance training performance and accelerate inference decoding. In particular, MTP has strong potential to boost RL rollout speed, which helps to scale LLMs towards greater intelligence.
With a lightweight dense Feed-Forward Network (FFN) and sliding window attention, our MTP block delivers substantial decoding speedups in practice at high acceptance rates.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The pre-training recipe of MiMo-V2-Flash largely follows that of MiMo-7B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xia et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, with several enhancements. Training is conducted using FP8 mixed-precision, enabling efficient large-scale training over 27T tokens. The model is initially pre-trained with a native 32K context and later extended to 256K. The resulting pretrained model, MiMo-V2-Flash-Base, has been evaluated against leading open-source base models such as Kimi-K2-Base <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kimi Team, 2025b</a>)</cite> and DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp-Base <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
MiMo-V2-Flash-Base achieves competitive performance across general benchmarks and surpasses peer models on reasoning-focused tasks.
For long-context retrieval, our hybrid attention architecture achieves nearly 100% success rates across context lengths from 32K to 256K. On the extreme long-context reasoning benchmark GSM-Infinite <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib71" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, MiMo-V2-Flash demonstrates robust performance with minimal degradation when scaling from 16K to 128K.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">In post-training, we focus on efficiently scaling RL compute to improve reasoning and agentic capabilities. To this end, MiMo-V2-Flash introduces a novel post-training paradigm termed Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD). This framework addresses both learning inefficiency and capability imbalance through a three-stage process: (1) general Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT); (2) specialized RL/SFT to train domain-specific teacher models; (3) MOPD, wherein the student model learns from two complementary signals: dense, token-level rewards from specialized teachers trained across diverse domains, and a verifiable, outcome-based reward. By integrating diverse expert knowledge in this manner, MiMo-V2-Flash simultaneously masters the peak capabilities of domain teachers while benefiting from stable and efficient learning dynamics.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">MiMo-V2-Flash achieves performance comparable
to that of Kimi-K2-Thinking and DeepSeek-V3.2-Thinking on most reasoning benchmarks.
In long-context evaluations such as LongBench V2 and MRCR, MiMo-V2-Flash consistently surpasses larger full-attention models, confirming the robustness of its hybrid SWA architecture. Notably, the model attains 73.4% on SWE-Bench Verified and 71.7% on SWE-Bench Multilingual, establishing it as the leading open-source model for software engineering tasks.
The model weights (with 3-layer MTP weights) are available at
<a href="https://github.com/XiaomiMiMo/MiMo-V2-Flash" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter" style="--ltx-fg-color:#FF6901;">https://github.com/XiaomiMiMo/MiMo-V2-Flash</a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>MiMo-V2-Flash Model Architecture</h2>

<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>Overall Architecture</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As illustrated in Figure <a href="#S2.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 2.1 Overall Architecture ‣ 2 MiMo-V2-Flash Model Architecture ‣ MiMo-V2-Flash Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, MiMo-V2-Flash follows a standard Transformer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Vaswani et al., 2017</a>)</cite> backbone augmented with MoE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shazeer et al., 2017</a>)</cite> and hybrid attention <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">Brown et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gemma Team, 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gemma Team, 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qwen Team, 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kimi Team, 2025c</a>)</cite>.
MiMo-V2-Flash is mainly composed of repeated hybrid blocks that interleave Local Sliding Window Attention (SWA) and Global Attention (GA).
It stacks <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M=8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M=8</annotation></semantics></math> hybrid blocks, each structured with <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N=5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N=5</annotation></semantics></math> consecutive SWA blocks followed by an GA block.
The only exception is the very first Transformer block, which uses global attention with a dense Feed-Forward Network (FFN) to stabilize early representation learning. The sliding window size <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>W</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W</annotation></semantics></math> used in MiMo-V2-Flash is <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="128" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>128</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">128</annotation></semantics></math>. Both the SWA block and the GA block utilize the sparse MoE FFN.
Each MoE layer comprises 256 experts in total, with 8 activated per token, and contains no shared experts.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">MiMo-V2-Flash also integrates MTP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gloeckle et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xia et al., 2025</a>)</cite> to improve model performance (both quality and efficiency). Worth noting, the MTP block uses dense FFN instead of MoE and applies SWA rather than GA, making it lightweight for speculative decoding. The number of parameters for each MTP block is only 0.33B.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F2" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2601.02780v2/mimo-v2-arch.svg" id="S2.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:381/326;" width="381" height="326"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S2.F2.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 2</span>: </span><span id="S2.F2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">An illustration of MiMo-V2-Flash model architecture. The model comprises <math id="S2.F2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M=8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M=8</annotation></semantics></math> Hybrid Blocks, where each Hybrid Block interleaves <math id="S2.F2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N=5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N=5</annotation></semantics></math> Sliding Window Attention (SWA) blocks with one Global Attention (GA) block. Both are equipped with a sparse MoE FFN. The only exception is the first block, which uses GA with a dense FFN. The MTP blocks employ SWA and a dense FFN.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="S2.T1" class="ltx_table">

<td id="S2.T1.3.10.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.T1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="192/128" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn mathsize="0.900em">192</mn><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em" stretchy="true" symmetric="true">/</mo><mn mathsize="0.900em">128</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">192/128</annotation></semantics></math></td></tr>

<td id="S2.T1.3.11.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb"><math id="S2.T1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.33" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn mathsize="0.900em">0.33</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.33</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S2.T1.3.11.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">B</span></td></tr>
</table>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 1: </span>Detailed model configuration of MiMo-V2-Flash.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S2.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S2.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 2.1 Overall Architecture ‣ 2 MiMo-V2-Flash Model Architecture ‣ MiMo-V2-Flash Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> summarizes detailed configurations of MiMo-V2-Flash. The model consists of 39 SWA layers and 9 GA layers. Both SWA and GA utilize Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ainslie et al., 2023</a>)</cite>. Specifically,
SWA has 64 query heads and 8 key-value heads, while GA has 64 query heads and 4 key-value heads. The per-head dimensions are the same for SWA and GA (192 for queries and keys, and 128 for values). Rotary Positional Embedding (RoPE,  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Su et al. (2024)</a></cite>) is partially applied to the first 64 dimensions query and key.
Following recent best practices, we adopt an FP8 mixed-precision framework similar to DeepSeek-V3 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
Specifically, we retain BF16 precision for the attention output projections, as well as for the embedding and output head parameters, while maintaining FP32 precision for the MoE router parameters.
This mixed-precision configuration improves numerical stability without materially impacting training efficiency or memory footprint.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>Hybrid Sliding Window Attention Architecture</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Sliding window attention <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Beltagy et al., 2020</a>)</cite> restricts each token’s attention scope to a local window rather than the entire sequence, thereby reducing both computational and memory complexity dramatically.
This naturally motivates hybrid attention architectures that interleave sliding window attention with global attention.
However, prior work has shown that overly aggressive use of SWA, such as very small sliding window sizes or high SWA:GA ratios, can lead to substantial degradation in model performance <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gemma Team, 2025</a>)</cite>, especially in long-context tasks.
Recently, the introduction of learnable attention sink bias, which allows the model to assign little or no attention to tokens when needed, has substantially enhanced the modeling capacity of SWA-based architectures <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Agarwal et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
While the precise theoretical underpinnings of the attention sink mechanism remain an active research area <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xiao et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gu et al., 2024b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qiu et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sun et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, we empirically observed that learnable attention sinks bias dramatically enhance the performance of hybrid SWA models, matching or even surpassing baselines with fully GA layers.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In MiMo-V2-Flash, our implementation follows the design used in gpt-oss <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Agarwal et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, where a learnable attention sink bias <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="sink\in\mathbb{R}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mi>ℝ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">sink\in\mathbb{R}</annotation></semantics></math> is applied to the denominator of softmax for each attention head. Specifically, let the attention logits between token <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>j</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j</annotation></semantics></math> of one single head be:</p>
<table id="S2.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{ij}=\frac{q_{i}k_{j}^{\top}}{\sqrt{d}}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>k</mi><mi>j</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup></mrow><msqrt><mi>d</mi></msqrt></mfrac></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{ij}=\frac{q_{i}k_{j}^{\top}}{\sqrt{d}},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS2.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{j}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the query of token <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math> and key of token <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>j</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j</annotation></semantics></math>, respectively, and <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math> is the head dimension.
The attention weights are then given by:</p>
<table id="S2.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{ij}=\frac{\exp\left(a_{ij}-m_{i}\right)}{\exp\left(sink-m_{i}\right)+\sum_{j^{\prime}}\exp\left(a_{ij^{\prime}}-m_{i}\right)}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>exp</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>m</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>exp</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>m</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.055em">+</mo><mrow><msub><mo>∑</mo><msup><mi>j</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></msub><mrow><mi>exp</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>j</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>m</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{ij}=\frac{\exp\left(a_{ij}-m_{i}\right)}{\exp\left(sink-m_{i}\right)+\sum_{j^{\prime}}\exp\left(a_{ij^{\prime}}-m_{i}\right)},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<table id="S2.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m_{i}=\max\left(\max_{j}a_{ij},\;sink\right)." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>m</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>max</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><munder><mi>max</mi><mi>j</mi></munder><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo rspace="0.447em">,</mo><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m_{i}=\max\left(\max_{j}a_{ij},\;sink\right).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Finally, the attention output for query <math id="S2.SS2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math> is obtained as a weighted sum over the values:</p>
<table id="S2.E4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="o_{i}=\sum_{j=1}^{n}s_{ij}v_{j}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">o_{i}=\sum_{j=1}^{n}s_{ij}v_{j}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS2.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">2.2.1 </span>Model Architecture Experiments</h4>

<div id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To validate the effectiveness of our design choice, we conduct exploratory and empirical studies on a 32B dense model, maintaining the query–key dimensions and rotary embedding configurations consistent with those described above.</p>

<td id="S2.T3.3.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_t"><span id="S2.T3.3.2.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">All GA</span></td>
<td id="S2.T3.3.2.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t"><span id="S2.T3.3.2.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">12.3</span></td>
<td id="S2.T3.3.2.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t"><span id="S2.T3.3.2.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">49.7</span></td>
<td id="S2.T3.3.2.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t"><span id="S2.T3.3.2.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">89.4</span></td>
<td id="S2.T3.3.2.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t"><span id="S2.T3.3.2.5.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">32.5</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S2.T3.3.3" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S2.T3.3.3.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left"><span id="S2.T3.3.3.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Hybrid SWA(<math id="S2.T3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W=128" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>W</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>128</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W=128</annotation></semantics></math>, w/ sink)</span></td>
<td id="S2.T3.3.3.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center"><span id="S2.T3.3.3.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">17.3</span></td>
<td id="S2.T3.3.3.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center"><span id="S2.T3.3.3.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">51.2</span></td>

<td id="S2.T3.3.4.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb"><span id="S2.T3.3.4.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">17.2</span></td>

</table>

</table>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 4: </span>Complex reasoning benchmark results for different attention configurations.</figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S2.SS2.SSS1.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Baselines and Benchmarks</h5>

<div id="S2.SS2.SSS1.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS1.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate four model architecture variants in a comparative setting. These include an all global attention (All GA) baseline, a hybrid SWA model with a 128-token window without attention sinks bias, and two hybrid SWA models augmented with attention sinks bias using window sizes of 128 and 512, respectively.
All variants share the same training pipeline: pre-training on 250B tokens with an 8,192 sequence length, long context extension to 32,768 over an additional 40B tokens, followed by long-context SFT and reasoning SFT with chain-of-thought supervision.
We evaluate model variants across benchmarks covering general capability, long-context understanding, and complex reasoning. General-domain results (Table <a href="#S2.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 2.2.1 Model Architecture Experiments ‣ 2.2 Hybrid Sliding Window Attention Architecture ‣ 2 MiMo-V2-Flash Model Architecture ‣ MiMo-V2-Flash Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>) are obtained from pre-trained base models without long-context extension, evaluating general knowledge and reasoning on MMLU <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hendrycks et al. (2021a)</a></cite>, BBH <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Suzgun et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, TriviaQA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Joshi et al., 2017</a>)</cite>, GSM8K <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cobbe et al., 2021</a>)</cite>, MATH <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hendrycks et al., 2021b</a>)</cite>, CMMLU <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib62" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, and MBPP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">Austin et al., 2021</a>)</cite>. Long-context results (Table <a href="#S2.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 2.2.1 Model Architecture Experiments ‣ 2.2 Hybrid Sliding Window Attention Architecture ‣ 2 MiMo-V2-Flash Model Architecture ‣ MiMo-V2-Flash Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>) evaluate long-context–extended base models on GSM-Infinite <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib71" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, NoLiMa <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Modarressi et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, and RULER-32k <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hsieh et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, and long-context SFT models on MRCR <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib78" title="" class="ltx_ref">Vodrahalli et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. For GSM-Infinite and Nolima, we construct internal few-shot benchmarks to assess base models under controlled long-context settings. Complex reasoning results (Table <a href="#S2.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ 2.2.1 Model Architecture Experiments ‣ 2.2 Hybrid Sliding Window Attention Architecture ‣ 2 MiMo-V2-Flash Model Architecture ‣ MiMo-V2-Flash Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>) evaluate the reasoning SFT models on AIME24&amp;25 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">MAA, 2024</a>)</cite>, LiveCodeBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jain et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, and GPQA-Diamond <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rein et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.SSS1.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS1.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We highlight our key empirical findings below:</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2.SSS1.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Ablation on Attention Sink Bias</h5>

<div id="S2.SS2.SSS1.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS1.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As shown in Table <a href="#S2.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 2.2.1 Model Architecture Experiments ‣ 2.2 Hybrid Sliding Window Attention Architecture ‣ 2 MiMo-V2-Flash Model Architecture ‣ MiMo-V2-Flash Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, hybrid SWA (<math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W=128" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>W</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>128</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W=128</annotation></semantics></math>, w/o sink) suffers noticeable performance degradation across general benchmarks, whereas introducing attention sink bias consistently recovers or improves performance relative to the all-GA baseline. Thus, in our further experiments, we assume that the attention sink bias is applied by default.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2.SSS1.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Sliding Window Attention Size</h5>

<div id="S2.SS2.SSS1.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS1.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Hybrid SWA (<math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W=128" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>W</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>128</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W=128</annotation></semantics></math>) and Hybrid SWA (<math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W=512" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>W</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>512</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W=512</annotation></semantics></math>) appear to perform similarly on general benchmarks (Table <a href="#S2.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 2.2.1 Model Architecture Experiments ‣ 2.2 Hybrid Sliding Window Attention Architecture ‣ 2 MiMo-V2-Flash Model Architecture ‣ MiMo-V2-Flash Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>). However, after long-context extension and long-context SFT, hybrid SWA (<math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.Px3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W=128" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>W</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>128</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W=128</annotation></semantics></math>) surpasses the all-GA baseline, whereas SWA (<math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.Px3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W=512" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>W</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>512</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W=512</annotation></semantics></math>) experiences significant degradation (Table <a href="#S2.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 2.2.1 Model Architecture Experiments ‣ 2.2 Hybrid Sliding Window Attention Architecture ‣ 2 MiMo-V2-Flash Model Architecture ‣ MiMo-V2-Flash Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2.SSS1.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Reasoning Ability</h5>

<div id="S2.SS2.SSS1.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS1.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As shown in Table <a href="#S2.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ 2.2.1 Model Architecture Experiments ‣ 2.2 Hybrid Sliding Window Attention Architecture ‣ 2 MiMo-V2-Flash Model Architecture ‣ MiMo-V2-Flash Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, hybrid SWA (<math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.Px4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W=128" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>W</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>128</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W=128</annotation></semantics></math>) surpasses the all-GA baseline across different challenging reasoning benchmarks, showing clear improvements on complex reasoning abilities.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">2.2.2 </span>Summary and Discussion</h4>

<div id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our experiments show that hybrid SWA (<math id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W=128" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>W</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>128</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W=128</annotation></semantics></math>) not only outperforms hybrid SWA (<math id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W=512" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>W</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>512</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W=512</annotation></semantics></math>) but can also surpass the all-GA baseline, which may seem counterintuitive. We hypothesize that this arises from a combination of better regularization and effective sparsity. Smaller windows force the model to focus on local context, serving as an inductive bias that mitigates overfitting on spurious patterns. Moreover, a tighter window (<math id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W=128" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>W</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>128</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W=128</annotation></semantics></math>) compels SWA to model local information while delegating long-range dependencies to the global attention layers, resulting in a clearer division of labor with more accurate and efficient learning. In contrast, a larger window (<math id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W=512" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>W</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>512</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W=512</annotation></semantics></math>) can blur this distinction, causing SWA to partially handle long-range dependencies itself, which dilutes the separation between local and global information and leads to suboptimal performance.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We emphasize that these observations and findings are empirical and derived from our specific experimental settings, including model scale, datasets, and training procedures.
Nonetheless, we hope these observations contribute an additional perspective to the ongoing discussion of efficient attention architectures in the era of reasoning and agentic AI models, and motivate further community-wide investigation into efficient architecture.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.3 </span>Lightweight Multi-Token Prediction (MTP)</h3>

<section id="S2.SS3.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">2.3.1 </span>Motivation of using MTP</h4>

<div id="S2.SS3.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Prior work demonstrates that MTP is a powerful training objective that enhances training efficiency and model quality <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gloeckle et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xia et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
Beyond these training benefits, we place stronger emphasis on exploiting MTP as a native draft model for self-speculative decoding to deliver real-deployment speedup.
In the following, we elaborate on how MTP accelerates inference from two perspectives: general LLM decoding speedup and RL training acceleration.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS3.SSS1.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Accelerating LLM Decoding</h5>

<div id="S2.SS3.SSS1.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.SSS1.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">LLM decoding is inherently memory-bound due to low arithmetic intensity. Batch-level parallelism is commonly used to increase FFN arithmetic intensity but does not benefit attention computation, as each request maintains its own KV cache. In contrast, MTP lifts the arithmetic intensity of both FFN and attention by generating multiple draft tokens, which the main model then verifies in parallel. This approach enables token-level parallelism without increasing KV cache I/O.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS3.SSS1.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Accelerating RL Training</h5>

<div id="S2.SS3.SSS1.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.SSS1.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">MTP acceleration is particularly well-suited for RL training <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">RadixArk Team, 2025</a>)</cite>, where the rollout phase consistently emerges as the dominant bottleneck due to the inference and decoding costs.
MTP addresses two key challenges in RL training:</p>
<ul id="S2.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S2.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">It enables efficient and effective RL with small batches.</span>
Current RL training relies on large-batch, off-policy algorithms to maximize throughput <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schulman et al., 2017</a>; <a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zheng et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
However, on-policy training is generally more stable and effective, yet its small batches underutilize GPU resources.
MTP mitigates this limitation by scaling token-level parallelism instead of batch size, making small-batch, on-policy RL training more practical.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">It mitigates GPU idleness from long-tail stragglers.</span>
As the rollout phase progresses, long-tail stragglers that process long sequences with small batch sizes (often approaching 1) can cause significant GPU idleness <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhong et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gao et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
In such scenarios, MTP enhances the computational efficiency of both attention and FFN, substantially reducing overall latency.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS3.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">2.3.2 </span>Lightweight MTP Design in MiMo-V2-Flash</h4>

<div id="S2.SS3.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In MiMo-V2-Flash, the MTP block is deliberately kept lightweight to prevent it from becoming a new inference bottleneck. We use a small dense FFN rather than MoE to limit parameter count, and employ SWA instead of Global Attention (GA) to reduce KV cache and attention computation costs.
During pre-training, only a single MTP head is attached to the model to avoid extra training overhead.
In post-training, this head is replicated <math id="S2.SS3.SSS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> times to form a <math id="S2.SS3.SSS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math>-step MTP module, and all heads are jointly trained for multi-step prediction.
Each head receives the main-model hidden state and token embedding as input, providing richer predictive information.
Despite its lightweight design, the MTP module remains highly effective and achieves a high acceptance rate.
Detailed results are presented in Section <a href="#S5" title="5 MTP Speedup ‣ MiMo-V2-Flash Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Pre-Training</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The MiMo-V2-Flash pre-training corpus consists of 27 trillion tokens drawn from a diverse collection of high-quality sources, including public web content, books, academic papers, code, mathematics, and broader STEM materials. Our data processing pipeline largely follows that of MiMo-7B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xia et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, with a deliberate shift toward data exhibiting long-range dependencies.
In particular, we emphasize long-form web documents and carefully curated code corpora such as repository-level code, pull requests, issues, and commit histories to strengthen the model’s ability to capture extended contextual relationships and perform complex, multi-step reasoning.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Data Scheduler</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The pre-training of MiMo-V2-Flash is organized into three sequential stages:</p>
<ul id="S3.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S3.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Stage 1 (Pre-training, 0 – 22T).</span> The model is trained on a diverse, high-quality general-purpose corpus using a context length of 32K tokens to establish strong foundational language capabilities.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Stage 2 (Mid-training, 22 – 26T).</span> We modify the data mixture by upsampling code-centric data and incorporating approximately 5% synthetic reasoning data to further enhance logical reasoning and program synthesis abilities.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Stage 3 (Context Extension, 26 – 27T).</span> Following the Stage 2 data distribution, we extend the model’s context window to 256K tokens and upsample data with long-range dependencies, enabling more effective modeling of extended contexts and long-horizon reasoning.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Hyper-Parameters</h3>

<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Model Hyper-Parameters</h5>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We configure MiMo-V2-Flash with 48 Transformer layers, comprising 39 sliding window attention layers and 9 global attention layers. The hidden dimension is set to 4096. All layers except the first are equipped with sparse MoE. Each MoE layer contains 256 routed experts, with 8 experts activated per token, and an intermediate hidden dimension of 2048 for each expert. The intermediate hidden dimension of the FFN of dense layers is set to 16384. All learnable parameters are randomly initialized with a standard deviation of 0.006. The model uses a single MTP layer during pre-training. Overall, MiMo-V2-Flash has 309B total parameters, of which 15B are active.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Training Hyper-Parameters</h5>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We employ the AdamW optimizer with <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta_{1}=0.9" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>β</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.9</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta_{1}=0.9</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta_{2}=0.95" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>β</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.95</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta_{2}=0.95</annotation></semantics></math>, and a weight decay of 0.1.
Gradient clipping is applied with a maximum norm of 1.0.
The learning rate schedule operates in two stages.
In Stage 1, the learning rate starts with a linear warm-up from 0 to <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3.2\times 10^{-4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>3.2</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3.2\times 10^{-4}</annotation></semantics></math> over the first 50B tokens, followed by a constant phase at <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3.2\times 10^{-4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>3.2</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3.2\times 10^{-4}</annotation></semantics></math> for 12T tokens, and concludes with a cosine decay to <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1.0\times 10^{-4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.0</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.0\times 10^{-4}</annotation></semantics></math> over 10T tokens. Stage 2 begins at <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1.0\times 10^{-4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.0</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.0\times 10^{-4}</annotation></semantics></math> and follows a cosine decay down to <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3.0\times 10^{-5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>3.0</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3.0\times 10^{-5}</annotation></semantics></math> over 4T tokens. The batch size warms up linearly to 2,048 over the initial 500B tokens and remains constant for the remainder of both stages.
Regarding auxiliary losses, the MoE sequence auxiliary loss coefficient is set to <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1.0\times 10^{-5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.0</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.0\times 10^{-5}</annotation></semantics></math> for all stages. The expert bias update factor is set to 0.001 during Stage 1 and Stage 2. The MTP loss weight is set to 0.3 for Stage 1 and 0.1 for Stage 2 and 3.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Long Context Extension</h5>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In Stage 1, we set the pre-training sequence length to 32,768 with a RoPE base frequency of 640,000 for GA and 10,000 for SWA. In Stage 3, the sequence length is extended to 262,144, and the RoPE base frequency of GA is adjusted to 5,000,000. The learning rate in Stage 3 decays from <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3.0\times 10^{-5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>3.0</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3.0\times 10^{-5}</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1.0\times 10^{-5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.0</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.0\times 10^{-5}</annotation></semantics></math> following a cosine schedule, with a fixed batch size of 256. The expert bias update factor is reduced to <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1.0\times 10^{-5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.0</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.0\times 10^{-5}</annotation></semantics></math> in Stage 3.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Evaluations</h3>

<section id="S3.SS3.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.3.1 </span>Evaluation Setup</h4>

<div id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate MiMo-V2-Flash-Base on a series of benchmarks, encompassing various capabilities: (1) General language understanding and reasoning, including BBH <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Suzgun et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, MMLU <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hendrycks et al., 2021a</a>)</cite>, MMLU-Redux <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gema et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, MMLU-Pro <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, DROP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dua et al., 2019</a>)</cite>, ARC <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Clark et al., 2018</a>)</cite>, HellaSwag <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zellers et al., 2019</a>)</cite>, WinoGrande <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sakaguchi et al., 2020</a>)</cite>, TriviaQA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Joshi et al., 2017</a>)</cite>, GPQA-Diamond <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rein et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, SuperGPQA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Du et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, and SimpleQA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib65" title="" class="ltx_ref">OpenAI, 2024</a>)</cite>.
(2) Mathematics reasoning.
GSM8K <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cobbe et al., 2021</a>)</cite>, MATH <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hendrycks et al., 2021b</a>)</cite>, and AIME <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">MAA, 2024</a>)</cite> (2024 &amp; 2025).
(3) Coding. HumanEval+ <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, MBPP+ <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, CRUXEval <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gu et al., 2024a</a>)</cite>, MultiPL-E <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib66" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cassano et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, BigCodeBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib67" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhuo et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, LiveCodeBench-v6 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jain et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, and SWE-Bench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib80" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jimenez et al., 2024b</a>)</cite> (few-shot Agentless Repair <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib70" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xia et al., 2024</a>)</cite>).
(4) Chinese understanding. C-Eval <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib61" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huang et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, CMMLU <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib62" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, and C-SimpleQA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib64" title="" class="ltx_ref">He et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
(5) Multilingual understanding. GlobalMMLU <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib68" title="" class="ltx_ref">Singh et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, and INCLUDE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib69" title="" class="ltx_ref">Romanou et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
(6) Long context. NIAH-Multi <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hsieh et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, GSM-Infinite <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib71" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2025</a>)</cite> (5-shot, Hard Ops-{2,4,6,8,10}).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.3.2 </span>Evaluation Results</h4>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 5: </span>
Comparison among MiMo-V2-Flash and other open-source base models. An asterisk (*) denotes that the model does not follow the format of few-shot examples.
</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS3.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S3.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ 3.3.2 Evaluation Results ‣ 3.3 Evaluations ‣ 3 Pre-Training ‣ MiMo-V2-Flash Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> presents a comprehensive comparison of MiMo-V2-Flash-Base against leading open-source base models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kimi Team, 2025b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
MiMo-V2-Flash-Base delivers competitive performance across most benchmarks and consistently outperforms peers on reasoning tasks (MMLU-Pro, GPQA-Diamond, AIME).
On SWE-Bench, it even surpasses the substantially larger Kimi-K2-Base while using less than one-third the parameters, underscoring the strength of our approach for realistic code-agent tasks.
However, constrained by its limited parameter count, we observe MiMo-V2-Flash exhibits lower knowledge capacity compared to larger models, as reflected in SimpleQA.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.T6" class="ltx_table">
<div id="S3.T6.3" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_center ltx_transformed_outer" style="width:341.6pt;height:112.2pt;vertical-align:-54.4pt;"><span class="ltx_transformed_inner" style="transform:translate(-52.0pt,17.1pt) scale(0.766476940557862,0.766476940557862) ;">
<table id="S3.T6.3.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_middle">
<tr id="S3.T6.3.1.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S3.T6.3.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_tt" rowspan="2"><span id="S3.T6.3.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Benchmark</span></td>

</span></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 6: </span>
Long context performance of MiMo-V2-Flash and other open-source base models. An asterisk (*) indicates the model may fail to follow the prompt. All baseline models have maximum model lengths shorter than 256K.
</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS3.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We illustrate the long context capabilities of each model in Table <a href="#S3.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ 3.3.2 Evaluation Results ‣ 3.3 Evaluations ‣ 3 Pre-Training ‣ MiMo-V2-Flash Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>.
For long-context retrieval, our model architecture achieves a near 100% success rate from 32K to 256K.
On the extreme stress long context reasoning benchmark GSM-Infinite, MiMo-V2-Flash also shows strong performance, with minimal performance degradation from 16K to 128K.
In contrast, DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp, a sparse attention LLM, attains the highest score under 32K but degrades substantially at 64K and 128K, suggesting an intrinsic disadvantage in long-context reasoning with noisy inputs.
These results strongly demonstrate the effectiveness and scalability of our hybrid SWA architecture, vanilla 32K pretraining, and context extension training.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Post-Training</h2>

<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD): A New Post-Training Paradigm</h3>

<figure id="S4.F3" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2601.02780v2/post-training.png" id="S4.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/189;" width="476" height="189" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F3.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 3</span>: </span><span id="S4.F3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Overview of MiMo-V2-Flash post-training stages.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Modern language models increasingly rely on extensive post-training to enhance their intelligence and capabilities. However, current post-training pipelines face fundamental challenges: <span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">capability imbalance</span>, where improving one skill causes regressions in others (the “see-saw” effect), and <span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">learning inefficiency</span>, where existing approaches fail to fully leverage training signals when combining knowledge from multiple specialized models.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We propose Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD), a unified post-training paradigm that addresses these challenges through a three-stage framework, as illustrated in Figure <a href="#S4.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 4.1 Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD): A New Post-Training Paradigm ‣ 4 Post-Training ‣ MiMo-V2-Flash Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>:</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Stage 1: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT)</h5>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We establish foundational instruction-following capabilities through supervised learning on high-quality instruction-response pairs, enabling the model to understand and execute user requests across diverse domains.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Stage 2: Domain-Specialized Training</h5>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We train a suite of domain-specialized teacher models through independent RL optimization on focused tasks including agentic capabilities (search, coding, general tool use) and non-agentic tasks (mathematical reasoning, general reasoning, safety alignment). Each teacher achieves superior performance in its respective domain through targeted optimization with domain-specific reward signals.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Stage 3: Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation</h5>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Rather than merging model parameters or generating static offline datasets from experts, we formulate multi-teacher knowledge integration as an on-policy reinforcement learning process. The student model samples from its own evolving distribution and receives token-level supervision from domain-specific teachers through KL divergence rewards <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gu et al., 2024c</a>; <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Agarwal et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lu and Lab, 2025</a>)</cite>, effectively combining specialized capabilities without the traditional trade-offs (Table <a href="#S4.T7" title="Table 7 ‣ Stage 3: Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation ‣ 4.1 Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD): A New Post-Training Paradigm ‣ 4 Post-Training ‣ MiMo-V2-Flash Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T7" class="ltx_table">
<table id="S4.T7.3" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_align_middle">
<tr id="S4.T7.3.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S4.T7.3.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_tt" rowspan="2"><span id="S4.T7.3.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Benchmark</span></td>
<td id="S4.T7.3.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt"><span id="S4.T7.3.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Student</span></td>
<td id="S4.T7.3.1.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt" rowspan="2"><span id="S4.T7.3.1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Best Teacher</span></td>
<td id="S4.T7.3.1.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt"><span id="S4.T7.3.1.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Student</span></td>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 7: </span>Benchmark results of MOPD. The model types of best teachers are tagged, including RL, SFT, and the student model itself.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">This unified framework offers several critical advantages over traditional post-training approaches:</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="S4.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S4.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Effective and Efficient.</span>
Unlike parameter merging or sequential training, which often trade off capabilities, MOPD preserves peak performance of the strongest teacher across all domains. Furthermore, on-policy distillation using dense, token-level rewards from teacher logits ensures stable credit assignment and rapid convergence. By learning from its own distribution, the student avoids the exposure bias and distribution mismatch common in off-policy methods trained on static datasets.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Modular and Scalable.</span> The choice of teacher model is highly flexible: it can be a specialized RL-derived model with strong capabilities, a different SFT model, or even the student model itself. The decoupled design enables easy integration of new teachers without restructuring the entire pipeline. Moreover, the framework works seamlessly with existing outcome reward models (ORMs) and is especially advantageous for complex agentic tasks, where setting up independent training pipelines would otherwise be cumbersome.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Iterative Co-Evolution.</span> MOPD naturally supports a teacher-student co-evolution cycle. Distilled student models can re-enter the specialized RL stage to produce stronger teachers, which in turn provide higher-quality supervision for the next generation of students, forming a self-reinforcing improvement cycle that enables sustained capability scaling.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">In the following subsections, we detail each stage of the MOPD paradigm, beginning with supervised fine-tuning (§<a href="#S4.SS2" title="4.2 Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) ‣ 4 Post-Training ‣ MiMo-V2-Flash Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.2</span></a>), followed by specialized RL for both agentic and non-agentic tasks (§<a href="#S4.SS3" title="4.3 Scaling Reinforcement Learning (RL) ‣ 4 Post-Training ‣ MiMo-V2-Flash Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.3</span></a>), and conclude with the technical formulation of the multi-teacher distillation mechanism (§<a href="#S4.SS4" title="4.4 Technical Formulation of MOPD ‣ 4 Post-Training ‣ MiMo-V2-Flash Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.4</span></a>).</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT)</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The SFT stage serves as the foundation of our post-training pipeline, transforming the base model into a helpful assistant capable of following instructions and responding effectively across diverse tasks. This stage is crucial for activating the model’s latent capabilities acquired during pre-training and aligning its outputs with desired formats and styles.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To achieve this, we curated millions of training samples spanning diverse domains, including general conversation, reasoning, coding, and agent tasks. These samples cover both thinking and non-thinking modes, with responses generated by our in-house domain-specialized model checkpoints. This diverse training mixture ensures comprehensive capability activation across the model’s intended use cases.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Through preliminary experiments, we identified a critical stability metric for MoE SFT training: the number of parameters with zero gradients (num-zeros). This metric provides early warning signals for training instability: an increasing num-zeros indicates deteriorating load balance among experts, while a decreasing num-zeros suggests the model is significantly overfitting to the training data. Maintaining stable num-zeros throughout training is therefore essential for successful SFT. Furthermore, this stability is paramount for ensuring the robustness and convergence of the subsequent RL phase.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Our experiments reveal that num-zeros stability critically depends on two hyperparameters: the expert bias update rate and the <math id="S4.SS2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϵ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon</annotation></semantics></math> parameter in the AdamW optimizer. Based on these findings, we configure our training with the following hyperparameters. We employ a cosine decay learning rate scheduler from <math id="S4.SS2.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5.0\times 10^{-5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>5.0</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5.0\times 10^{-5}</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S4.SS2.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5.0\times 10^{-6}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>5.0</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5.0\times 10^{-6}</annotation></semantics></math>, with a batch size of 128 and AdamW <math id="S4.SS2.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϵ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon</annotation></semantics></math> set to <math id="S4.SS2.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1.0\times 10^{-8}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.0</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.0\times 10^{-8}</annotation></semantics></math>. The MoE expert bias update rate is set to <math id="S4.SS2.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1.0\times 10^{-4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.0</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.0\times 10^{-4}</annotation></semantics></math>, and the sequence auxiliary loss coefficient to <math id="S4.SS2.p4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1.0\times 10^{-6}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.0</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.0\times 10^{-6}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Scaling Reinforcement Learning (RL)</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Reinforcement learning pushes model capabilities beyond what supervised fine-tuning alone can achieve.
We employ different RL strategies depending on whether tasks involve agentic behavior, scaling both non-agentic and agentic RL training to maximize performance across diverse domains.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS3.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.3.1 </span>Non-Agentic RL Training</h4>

<div id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Non-agentic RL training focuses on improving the model’s performance on single-turn tasks, where the model generates a complete response without requiring interactive feedback or multi-step execution. The primary objective is to enhance the model’s reasoning accuracy in verifiable domains (e.g., mathematics, coding, logic) while simultaneously aligning its outputs for helpfulness and safety in open-ended conversations.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Our approach to generating reward signals varies based on task characteristics. For domains with verifiable outcomes, we employ a hybrid verification system combining programmatic tools with an LLM judge to automatically assess correctness against curated problem-solution pairs.
For subjective qualities such as helpfulness and safety, we implement a rubric-based framework where an advanced LLM judge evaluates responses against detailed rubrics and reference answers, producing granular reward signals that guide the model toward desired behaviors.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.3.2 </span>Agentic RL Training</h4>

<figure id="S4.T8" class="ltx_table">
