</figure>
<div id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">While non-agentic RL focuses on single-turn reasoning and generation, agentic RL trains the model to operate in interactive, multi-turn environments requiring planning, action execution, and adaptation based on feedback. We scale agentic RL along two critical dimensions: environment diversity and compute resources.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS3.SSS2.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Scaling Agentic Environment Diversity</h5>

<div id="S4.SS3.SSS2.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS2.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We construct a diverse suite of agentic training environments spanning code debugging, terminal operations, web development, and general tool use (Table <a href="#S4.T8" title="Table 8 ‣ 4.3.2 Agentic RL Training ‣ 4.3 Scaling Reinforcement Learning (RL) ‣ 4 Post-Training ‣ MiMo-V2-Flash Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>). Each environment targets distinct capabilities while sharing the common requirement of multi-step reasoning and execution. Below, we elaborate on the details for agentic environments.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3.SSS2.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Code Agent</h5>

<div id="S4.SS3.SSS2.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS2.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We train on large-scale code agentic tasks derived from real-world GitHub issues, where the model operates in an agentic loop to read and edit files, execute commands, and receive rewards based on verifiable unit tests. Our key insight is that continuously scaling available tasks drives sustained improvements in code intelligence. To enable efficient RL training on over 100,000 code tasks, we develop two infrastructure components. First, we build an automated environment setup pipeline that provisions development environments from repository snapshots and packages them into containerized images, achieving 70% success rate across 8 programming languages and supported by a large-scale Kubernetes cluster running over 10,000 concurrent pods. Second, we implement a lightweight agent scaffold that integrates seamlessly with Kubernetes, Docker, or local backends, exposing three atomic tools (<span id="S4.SS3.SSS2.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">bash</span>, <span id="S4.SS3.SSS2.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">str_replace</span>, <span id="S4.SS3.SSS2.Px2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">finish</span>) that interact with execution backends solely via shell commands. This design eliminates server-based tool implementations and employs a minimal system prompt without predefined workflows, allowing the model to discover best practices during training.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3.SSS2.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Terminal Agent</h5>

<div id="S4.SS3.SSS2.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS2.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Beyond GitHub issues, we strengthen terminal-based problem-solving capabilities using tasks sourced from Stack Overflow and Stack Exchange. We select materials requiring advanced technical expertise and transform them into computational tasks with corresponding queries, Dockerfiles, and test cases. After verifying environment installation and filtering by difficulty and reliability, we obtain approximately 30,000 queries with validated execution environments. Additional filtering based on pass rates removes tasks with unreliable correctness judgments or insufficient complexity for effective RL training.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3.SSS2.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Web Development Agent</h5>

<div id="S4.SS3.SSS2.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS2.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To improve web development code generation, we build a real-world-grounded synthetic dataset paired with a multimodal verifier. We collect high-quality user-written web pages, execute generated code using Playwright to obtain rendered videos, and apply a multimodal visual discriminator to retain only high-quality samples, where video-based evaluation reduces visual hallucination compared to static screenshots. We reverse-engineer user queries from curated pages as seed prompts to synthesize large-scale RL data covering eight web categories that closely match real-world usage. Our vision-based verifier scores rollout executions from recorded videos, jointly evaluating visual quality, functional correctness, and executability to ensure rewards reflect both appearance and behavior.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3.SSS2.Px5" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">General Agent</h5>

<div id="S4.SS3.SSS2.Px5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS2.Px5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We develop two general agentic capabilities. Our search agent adopts a scaffold providing three core tools (search, open, find) for autonomous web exploration. We construct queries through recursive fact-graph expansion from seed entities, where difficulty scales with relation chain depth and detail obfuscation, enabling automated generation of challenging search problems with verifiable answers. Our function-calling agent trains on synthetic application environments with custom toolsets constructed by generating tool-call graphs based on explicit data dependencies (direct input-output relationships) and implicit logical dependencies (reasoning about hidden system states), requiring both data propagation and state inference capabilities.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3.SSS2.Px6" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Scaling Agentic Compute</h5>

<div id="S4.SS3.SSS2.Px6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS2.Px6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Training on the previous diverse set of agentic environments (Table <a href="#S4.T8" title="Table 8 ‣ 4.3.2 Agentic RL Training ‣ 4.3 Scaling Reinforcement Learning (RL) ‣ 4 Post-Training ‣ MiMo-V2-Flash Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>), we find that scaling agentic RL compute not only boosts code-agentic performance but also generalizes effectively to other task types. Figure <a href="#S4.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ Scaling Agentic Compute ‣ 4.3.2 Agentic RL Training ‣ 4.3 Scaling Reinforcement Learning (RL) ‣ 4 Post-Training ‣ MiMo-V2-Flash Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> shows the RL training curve for our code-agent, where the model performed on-policy rollouts and updates across approximately 120K environments.
This scaling significantly improves upon the SFT base model’s performance on SWE-Bench-Verified and SWE-Bench-Multilingual. Moreover, Figure <a href="#S4.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ Scaling Agentic Compute ‣ 4.3.2 Agentic RL Training ‣ 4.3 Scaling Reinforcement Learning (RL) ‣ 4 Post-Training ‣ MiMo-V2-Flash Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> demonstrates that large-scale code-agentic RL training generalizes effectively to other agentic tasks, as well as math, code, and general reasoning benchmarks, suggesting that agentic training develops broadly transferable problem-solving capabilities.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F4" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2601.02780v2/swebench_scaling.svg" id="S4.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:452/153;" width="452" height="153"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F4.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 4</span>: </span><span id="S4.F4.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Code-agentic RL scaling curves. The X-axis represents total interactive environments consumed during on-policy RL rollouts; the Y-axis shows resolved rates on SWE-Bench-Verified and SWE-Bench-Multilingual.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="S4.F5" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2601.02780v2/swe_generalization.svg" id="S4.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/213;" width="476" height="213"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F5.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 5</span>: </span><span id="S4.F5.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Generalization of code-agentic RL training to other task domains.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.4 </span>Technical Formulation of MOPD</h3>

<div id="S4.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Having established the foundation through SFT and trained specialized teachers through domain-specific RL, we now formalize the multi-teacher on-policy distillation mechanism that integrates these specialized capabilities into a unified student model.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Specifically, we cast multi-teacher distillation as an on-policy reinforcement learning objective. Let <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the target student policy optimized in the training engine, <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>μ</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the student sampling policy adopted in the inference engine, and <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{\text{domain}_{x}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><msub><mtext>domain</mtext><mi>x</mi></msub></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{\text{domain}_{x}}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the teacher policy specialized for the domain of prompt <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> sampled from distribution <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}</annotation></semantics></math>. Let <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{sg}[\cdot]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext>sg</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{sg}[\cdot]</annotation></semantics></math> denote the stop-gradient operator. The reverse KL divergence loss between student and teacher is defined as:</p>
<table id="S4.E5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E5.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\text{reverse-KL}}(\theta)=-\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D},y_{t}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x,y_{&lt;t})}\log\frac{\pi_{\text{domain}_{x}}(y_{t}|x,y_{&lt;t})}{\pi_{\theta}(y_{t}|x,y_{&lt;t})}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>reverse-KL</mtext></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0em">=</mo><mo lspace="0em">−</mo><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>∼</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>∼</mo><mi>π</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><mi>log</mi><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>π</mi><msub><mtext>domain</mtext><mi>x</mi></msub></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\text{reverse-KL}}(\theta)=-\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D},y_{t}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x,y_{&lt;t})}\log\frac{\pi_{\text{domain}_{x}}(y_{t}|x,y_{&lt;t})}{\pi_{\theta}(y_{t}|x,y_{&lt;t})}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(5)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS4.p2.2" class="ltx_p">The gradient is:</p>
<table id="S4.E6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E6.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\text{reverse-KL}}(\theta)=-\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D},y_{t}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x,y_{&lt;t})}\left[\log\frac{\pi_{\text{domain}_{x}}(y_{t}|x,y_{&lt;t})}{\pi_{\theta}(y_{t}|x,y_{&lt;t})}\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{t}|x,y_{&lt;t})\right]." class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>∼</mo><mi>π</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" lspace="0.167em" rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><mi>θ</mi></msub><mi>log</mi><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo fence="false" lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\text{reverse-KL}}(\theta)=-\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D},y_{t}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x,y_{&lt;t})}\left[\log\frac{\pi_{\text{domain}_{x}}(y_{t}|x,y_{&lt;t})}{\pi_{\theta}(y_{t}|x,y_{&lt;t})}\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{t}|x,y_{&lt;t})\right].</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(6)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS4.p2.3" class="ltx_p">Following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib72" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhao et al. (2025)</a></cite>, we apply training-inference importance sampling and discard tokens that exhibit large discrepancies. We then define the surrogate loss of MOPD as:</p>
<table id="S4.E7" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>

<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(7)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS4.p2.4" class="ltx_p">where</p>

0,&amp;\text{other},\end{cases}\quad\ \hat{A}_{\text{MOPD},t}=\text{sg}\left[\log\frac{\pi_{\text{domain}_{x}}(y_{t}|x,y_{&lt;t})}{\pi_{\theta}(y_{t}|x,y_{&lt;t})}\right].</annotation></semantics></math></td>

<div id="S4.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">By default, we combine the advantages of MOPD with other types of advantages, such as those computed using Outcome Reward Models (ORMs), including GRPO <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shao et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
Let <math id="S4.SS4.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{A}_{\text{ORM}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>A</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mtext>ORM</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{A}_{\text{ORM}}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the advantages computed by the ORMs; the final advantages are given by:</p>
<table id="S4.E9" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{A}_{\text{MOPD},t}=\text{sg}\left[\log\frac{\pi_{\text{domain}_{x}}(y_{t}|x,y_{&lt;t})}{\pi_{\theta}(y_{t}|x,y_{&lt;t})}\right]+\alpha\hat{A}_{\text{ORM}}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>A</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mtext>MOPD</mtext><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mtext>sg</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>π</mi><msub><mtext>domain</mtext><mi>x</mi></msub></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>A</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mtext>ORM</mtext></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{A}_{\text{MOPD},t}=\text{sg}\left[\log\frac{\pi_{\text{domain}_{x}}(y_{t}|x,y_{&lt;t})}{\pi_{\theta}(y_{t}|x,y_{&lt;t})}\right]+\alpha\hat{A}_{\text{ORM}}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(9)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F6.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 6</span>: </span><span id="S4.F6.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Comparison of different post-training methods on math and code tasks. Three lines represent training RL with ORM, MOPD without outcome rewards (MOPD w/o ORM), and MOPD. </span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS4.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S4.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ 4.4 Technical Formulation of MOPD ‣ 4 Post-Training ‣ MiMo-V2-Flash Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> demonstrates the effectiveness of MOPD compared to traditional post-training approaches. On mathematical reasoning (AIME 2025) and coding (LiveCodeBench) benchmarks, MOPD successfully preserves and combines specialized capabilities from multiple teachers, achieving performance that matches or exceeds the strongest teacher in most domains.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.5 </span>Evaluations</h3>

<section id="S4.SS5.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.5.1 </span>Evaluation Setup</h4>

<div id="S4.SS5.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate MiMo-V2-Flash on MMLU-Pro <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, GPQA-Diamond <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rein et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, HLE Text-only <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib73" title="" class="ltx_ref">Phan et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, AIME 2025 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">MAA, 2024</a>)</cite>, LiveCodeBench (2024.08-2025.04) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jain et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, HMMT Feb. 2025 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib76" title="" class="ltx_ref">Balunović et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, Arena-Hard <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib79" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, LongBench V2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib77" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bai et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, MRCR <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib78" title="" class="ltx_ref">Vodrahalli et al., 2024</a>)</cite> ({2,4,8}-needles, maximum 128K), SWE-Bench Verified <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jimenez et al., 2024a</a>)</cite>, SWE-Bench Multilingual <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, Terminal-Bench, BrowseComp <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib75" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, <math id="S4.SS5.SSS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>τ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>-Bench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib74" title="" class="ltx_ref">Barres et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS5.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.5.2 </span>Evaluation Results</h4>

<div id="S4.SS5.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We illustrate the evalution results in Table <a href="#S4.T9" title="Table 9 ‣ 4.5.2 Evaluation Results ‣ 4.5 Evaluations ‣ 4 Post-Training ‣ MiMo-V2-Flash Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a>.
MiMo-V2-Flash achieves performance comparable to that of Kimi-K2-Thinking and DeepSeek-V3.2-Thinking on most reasoning benchmarks.
The model also maintains competitive general writing capabilities, enabling it to generate high-quality responses on open-ended tasks.
In long context evaluations, our model surpasses Kimi-K2-Thinking, a significantly larger full global attention LLM, highlighting the strong long-context capabilities of our hybrid SWA architecture.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS5.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.SSS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Notably, MiMo-V2-Flash achieves 73.4% on SWE-Bench Verified, outperforming all open-source competitors and approaching the performance of GPT-5-High.
On SWE-Bench Multilingual, our model resolves 71.7% issues, establishing it as the most capable open-source LLM for software engineering tasks.
These results underscore the effectiveness of our ultra-scaled agentic RL training. On Terminal Bench, the model also delivers a competitive score.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS5.SSS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.SSS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In search agent evaluation, MiMo-V2-Flash scores 45.4 on BrowseComp, and is further boosted to 58.3 with the context management method outlined in Appendix <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Context Management ‣ MiMo-V2-Flash Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a>.
For general tool-use on <math id="S4.SS5.SSS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>τ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>-Bench, we employ DeepSeek-V3.2 as the user agent, achieving category scores of 95.3 (Telecom), 79.5 (Retail), 66.0 (Airline).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS5.SSS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.SSS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Taken together, these results validate the effectiveness of our ultra-large-scale RL training within the MOPD post-training paradigm, and highlight the models strong potential for real-world coding, reasoning, and agentic workflows.</p>
</div>

<section id="S4.SS6" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.6 </span>RL Infrastructures</h3>

<div id="S4.SS6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our RL (and MOPD) infrastructure uses SGLang <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zheng et al., 2024</a>)</cite> as the inference engine and Megatron-LM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shoeybi et al., 2019</a>)</cite> as the training engine.
We adopt FP8 for both training and inference.
To enable stable, efficient, and flexible RL training, we implement three extended modules: Rollout Routing Replay <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ma et al., 2025</a>)</cite> (Sec <a href="#S4.SS6.SSS1" title="4.6.1 Stablized Training via Rollout Routing Replay (R3) ‣ 4.6 RL Infrastructures ‣ 4 Post-Training ‣ MiMo-V2-Flash Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.6.1</span></a>), Data Scheduler (Sec <a href="#S4.SS6.SSS2" title="4.6.2 Data Scheduler ‣ 4.6 RL Infrastructures ‣ 4 Post-Training ‣ MiMo-V2-Flash Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.6.2</span></a>), and Tool Manager combined with Toolbox (Sec <a href="#S4.SS6.SSS3" title="4.6.3 Toolbox and Tool Manager ‣ 4.6 RL Infrastructures ‣ 4 Post-Training ‣ MiMo-V2-Flash Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.6.3</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS6.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.6.1 </span>Stablized Training via Rollout Routing Replay (R3)</h4>

<div id="S4.SS6.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS6.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">MoE models suffer from inconsistent expert routing across rollout and training due to numerical precision issues <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">He and Lab, 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yao et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
We propose Rollout Routing Replay (R3) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ma et al., 2025</a>)</cite> to train RL using the same routed experts from rollout, making its overhead negligible through optimized data types and communication overlapping.
For multi-turn agent training, we employ a request-level prefix cache during rollout.
This cache stores KVCache and MoE routed experts from prior turns, allowing them to be reused for subsequent generation steps of the same request.
Unlike the commonly-used radix cache in current inference engines, our request-level prefix cache avoids re-prefilling or inter-request output cache sharing, ensuring sampling consistency for routed experts.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS6.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.6.2 </span>Data Scheduler</h4>

<div id="S4.SS6.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS6.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For MiMo-V2-Flash, we extend the Seamless Rollout Engine <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xia et al., 2025</a>)</cite> and implement a Data Scheduler to seamlessly schedule fine-grained sequences instead of micro-batches, addressing GPU idleness in distributed MoE training.
In dynamic sampling, as sequences return for reward computation, we reference historical pass rates and, if necessary, assign new prompts to GPUs with load balancing.
We integrate partial rollout <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kimi Team, 2025a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fu et al., 2025</a>)</cite> to partition overlong trajectories across steps, while limiting staleness and the proportion of partial samples in each batch.
By employing staleness-aware truncated importance sampling for partial rollout, we significantly accelerate RL training without sacrificing model quality.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS6.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS6.SSS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The Data Scheduler supports data source-specific configurations (sample quota, scheduling priority, length limits, temperature) and fits pass rates to accept samples by configured ratios.
Priority-based scheduling overlaps reward computation and inference across data sources with different time patterns, ensuring high GPU utilization.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS6.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.6.3 </span>Toolbox and Tool Manager</h4>

<div id="S4.SS6.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS6.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We implement Toolbox and Tool Manager to tackle global resource contention and local inefficiency in RL agent training.
These modules leverage Ray <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">Moritz et al., 2018</a>)</cite> for efficient scheduling.
Toolbox acts as the centralized resource allocator, enforcing resource quota and QPS limits for tools across concurrent tasks.
It adopts fault-tolerant Ray actor pools, which eliminate cold-start delays.
Integrated with the rollout engine, Tool Manager coordinates with Toolbox to accelerate training through environment pre-warming and sequence-level asynchronous reward computation.
It maintains training stability through timeout recovery and real-time monitoring.
By disaggregating the tool management and rollout workflow, Toolbox isolates task-specific logic from system-wide policies, enabling modular extensibility without compromising stability.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>MTP Speedup</h2>

<section id="S5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.1 </span>MTP Acceptance Length</h3>

<div id="S5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We analyze the relationship between the model’s predictive uncertainty measured by next
token cross-entropy and the efficiency of the Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) module. As illustrated in Figure <a href="#S5.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ 5.1 MTP Acceptance Length ‣ 5 MTP Speedup ‣ MiMo-V2-Flash Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>, we evaluate the average acceptance length with 3 MTP layers across diverse benchmarks, ranging from code generation (e.g., WebDev, LiveCodeBench) to complex reasoning tasks (e.g., AIME25, MMLU Pro).</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F7" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2601.02780v2/entropy_vs_accept_length.svg" id="S5.F7.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:286/191;" width="286" height="191"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S5.F7.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 7</span>: </span><span id="S5.F7.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">The correlation between next token cross-entropy and Average Accept Length across different datasets. The orange dashed line represents the best-fit curve (<math id="S5.F7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R^{2}=0.995" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>0.995</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R^{2}=0.995</annotation></semantics></math>).</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S5.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The results reveal a strong inverse correlation: lower entropy contexts (such as WebDev) allow for significantly longer acceptance sequences, reaching approximately 3.6 tokens. Conversely, tasks with higher intrinsic uncertainty (e.g., MMLU Pro) exhibit shorter acceptance lengths due to increased prediction divergence. This behavior is accurately modeled by a log-transformed fit (<math id="S5.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y=4(1-0.58x^{0.58})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn>0.58</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>0.58</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y=4(1-0.58x^{0.58})</annotation></semantics></math>) with an <math id="S5.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> of <math id="S5.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.995" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.995</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.995</annotation></semantics></math>, suggesting that next token cross-entropy is a primary determinant of MTP throughput.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.2 </span>MTP Inference Speedup</h3>

<div id="S5.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We measure the decoding speedup of MiMo-V2-Flash with 3-layer MTP across varying batch sizes (per node) and accept lengths, using 16K input and 1K output lengths.
The results in Table <a href="#S5.T10" title="Table 10 ‣ 5.2 MTP Inference Speedup ‣ 5 MTP Speedup ‣ MiMo-V2-Flash Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a> demonstrate that MTP consistently outperforms the baseline without additional hardware costs.
Notably, the speedup scales linearly with accept length.
Under different batch sizes, MTP exhibits varying speedup, which depends on the corresponding computation and I/O demands as well as kernel efficiency.
In practice, researchers and engineers should tune both batch size and MTP layers based on hardware roofline models to optimize the speed-cost trade-off.</p>
</div>

</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Conclusion, Limitation, and Future Work</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">MiMo-V2-Flash achieves strong reasoning and agentic capabilities, along with fast inference speed, through its hybrid Sliding Window Attention architecture, lightweight Multi-Token Prediction, and the MOPD post-training paradigm. With these strengths, MiMo-V2-Flash rivals larger open-weight models like DeepSeek-V3.2 and Kimi-K2.
However, a clear gap remains to the strongest closed-weight models, which we aim to narrow by scaling model size and training compute.
Additionally, our current architectural exploration remains preliminary, with limited analysis of design trade-offs.
Future work will focus on designing more robust and efficient, agentic-oriented model architectures.
Furthermore, we plan to scale the compute for the iterative co-evolution of teachers and students in MOPD to fully unlock its potential.</p>
</div>
</section>

<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Reward Hacking of SWE-Bench</h2>

<div id="A2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Consistent with recent findings within the SWE-Bench community, we similarly identify the bug in the official SWE-Bench images where the ground truth commits are not properly deleted. During the RL training, this could lead to reward hacking and inflated evaluation, where the model tends to obtain rewards by peeking at future commits, as shown in Figure <a href="#A2.F8" title="Figure 8 ‣ Appendix B Reward Hacking of SWE-Bench ‣ MiMo-V2-Flash Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>. To fix this, we update to the newest SWE-Bench image for evaluation. For our self-built training images, we also follow the official SWE-Bench resolution on git hacking, and repeatedly confirm that our model does not exhibit any reward hacking.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A2.F8" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2601.02780v2/git_hack_all.svg" id="A2.F8.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:333/166;" width="333" height="166"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A2.F8.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 8</span>: </span><span id="A2.F8.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">The tendency of our experiment on Qwen3-32B to exhibit reward hacking during RL training within unprocessed images. We quantify the model’s git hacking attempts by counting a set of keywords, such as "<span id="A2.F8.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">git log ---all</span>", within the model’s rollout trajectories.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="A3" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix C </span>Context Management</h2>

<div id="A3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">While fine-tuning and reinforcement learning optimize model parameters <math id="A3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math>, context management strategically refines the conditioning context C in <math id="A3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P(y\mid C,\theta)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(y\mid C,\theta)</annotation></semantics></math>. Our approach addresses two complementary challenges. For context augmentation, we adopt a Unix-inspired abstraction: tools, documents, and databases are uniformly exposed as files, enabling the model to retrieve information via Bash commands—leveraging its native code-generation capabilities. For context consolidation, we combat the "Lost in the Middle" phenomenon by enforcing aggressive memory compression. When context utilization exceeds a threshold (as low as 30%), the system prompts the model to summarize, archives the full history to a retrievable memory file, and replaces active context with the summary. Empirically, this yields 5–10% accuracy gains on Deep Research tasks. Our results align with DeepSeek V3’s finding that discarding tool-call history outperforms retention strategies; replicating their aggressive reset protocol, we achieve 58.3 on comparable benchmarks. The core insight is counterintuitive: less context, strategically managed, produces more focused and accurate generation.</p>
</div>
</section>
</article>

              d="M224 160C224 107 267 64 320 64C373 64 416 107 416 160L416 163.6C416 179.3 403.3 192 387.6 192L252.5 192C236.8 192 224.1 179.3 224.1 163.6L224.1 160zM569.6 172.8C580.2 186.9 577.3 207 563.2 217.6L465.4 290.9C470.7 299.8 474.7 309.6 477.2 320L576 320C593.7 320 608 334.3 608 352C608 369.7 593.7 384 576 384L480 384L480 416C480 418.6 479.9 421.3 479.8 423.9L563.2 486.4C577.3 497 580.2 517.1 569.6 531.2C559 545.3 538.9 548.2 524.8 537.6L461.7 490.3C438.5 534.5 395.2 566.5 344 574.2L344 344C344 330.7 333.3 320 320 320C306.7 320 296 330.7 296 344L296 574.2C244.8 566.5 201.5 534.5 178.3 490.3L115.2 537.6C101.1 548.2 81 545.3 70.4 531.2C59.8 517.1 62.7 497 76.8 486.4L160.2 423.9C160.1 421.3 160 418.7 160 416L160 384L64 384C46.3 384 32 369.7 32 352C32 334.3 46.3 320 64 320L162.8 320C165.3 309.6 169.3 299.8 174.6 290.9L76.8 217.6C62.7 207 59.8 186.9 70.4 172.8C81 158.7 101.1 155.8 115.2 166.4L224 248C236.3 242.9 249.8 240 264 240L376 240C390.2 240 403.7 242.8 416 248L524.8 166.4C538.9 155.8 559 158.7 569.6 172.8z" />
          </svg>)</span> button, located in the page header.</li>
    </ul>
    <p><strong>Tip:</strong> You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.</p>
    <p>Our team has already identified <a class="ltx_ref" href="https://github.com/arXiv/html_feedback/issues"
        target="_blank">the following issues</a>. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we
      may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability
      should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for
      all.</p>
    <p>Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a <a
        class="ltx_ref" href="https://github.com/brucemiller/LaTeXML/wiki/Porting-LaTeX-packages-for-LaTeXML"
        target="_blank">list of packages that need conversion</a>, and welcome <a class="ltx_ref"
        href="https://github.com/brucemiller/LaTeXML/issues" target="_blank">developer contributions</a>.</p>
